sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Auðhumla** (*audhumla*) ​— Primeval ‌Cow, Nourisher ‌of Creation ​· the Cow ​of the ​Void — ​belongs to ​the Norse tradition, ‌where she ​is catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Primeval Cow, ​Nourisher of ‌Creation". The ​name means ‌"Wealth-humla (primeval cow)".[^1]

​Auðhumla is ​one of ​the earliest ​beings in Norse ​cosmogony. She ‌emerges from ​the melting ‌rime of Ginnungagap ​at the ‌dawn of ​time and ‌nourishes the primordial ​giant [[ymir|Ymir]] ‌with her ​milk. While ​Ymir sleeps, she ‌licks the ‌salty rime-stones ‌for three ​days and reveals ​a man: ‌Búri, the ​first of ​the gods and ‌grandfather of ​[[odinn|Óðinn]]. Without ​Auðhumla there ‌is no Búri, ​no Borr, ‌no Óðinn, ​and no ​world shaped from ​Ymir's body.[^2] ​She is ‌therefore the ‌silent generative power ​behind the ‌whole mythology ​of the ​Æsir.

PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as **Auðhumla** ‌and serves ‌its temple at ​[auðhumla.com](https://punicodex.com/audhumla/). The ‌restoration preserves ​the eth ​(ð) and the ​distinctive vowel ‌quality that ​the ASCII ​form loses, and ​exactly one ‌historically valid ​Unicode restoration ​exists, which places ​the name ‌in Tier ​1. The ‌plain ASCII form ​*audhumla* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by the ‌early domain-name ​system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete.[^1]

Poetic Edda (Eddukvæði), ed. Neckel-Kuhn; trans. Carolyn Larrington, Oxford World's Classics (2014), 1270.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Old ‌Norse as **Auðhumla**. ​Etymologically it ​means "Wealth-humla ​(primeval cow)"[^1]. The ​first element, ​**auð-**, can ‌mean 'wealth, prosperity' ​or 'desolate, ​empty' depending on ‌context; in ​the name ‌of the primeval ​cow it ‌is usually ​interpreted as 'wealth' ​or as ​the void ​from which she ​emerges. The ‌second element, ​**-humla**, is obscure ‌and possibly ​a by-form ‌related to words ​for cattle ‌or humming sound. ​Cleasby–Vigfússon and ‌Zoëga record ​the name without ​a settled ‌etymology.[^2]

The ‌ASCII form *audhumla* ‌survives only ​because the ​early domain-name system ‌could not ​carry diacritics; ​it is a ‌technological compromise, ​not an ​ancient spelling. The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Auðhumla** recovers the ‌voiced dental ​fricative eth ​(ð) directly in ​the address ​bar. The ‌original carries a ‌distinctive letter, ​and exactly ‌one historically valid ​Unicode restoration ​exists, which ‌places the name ‌in Tier ‌1.

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation runs:

​- **a** ‌→ **A** — ​Same, capitalized
​- **u** ​→ **u** — ‌Same
- ​**d** → ​**ð** — Eth: ​voiced dental ‌fricative
- ​**h** → **h** ​— Same
​- **u** ‌→ **u** — ​Same
- ‌**m** → ​**m** — Same
‌- **l** ​→ **l** — ‌Same
- ‌**a** → ​**a** — Same

​The project ​holds the ​domain **auðhumla.com** as ‌the canonical ‌home of ​this name.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 5, trans. Faulkes.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed., s.v. Auðhumla.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the name ​is ​**/ˈauðˌhum.la/** — ​Old ​Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme ‌by phoneme:

​- ​**Auð-** — ‌Diphthong ​[au] followed ‌by ​voiced dental ‌fricative ​[ð]; the ​first ​syllable carries ​stress
​- **-hum-** ‌— Short ​[u], ‌voiced bilabial ​nasal ‌[m], and ​voiceless ‌glottal fricative ​[h]
‌- **-la** ​— ​Lateral [l] ‌plus ‌short open ‌back ​[a], the ​weak ‌feminine ending

​For ​the modern ‌speaker, ​the closest ​approximation ‌is: 'OWTH-hoom-la' ​— ‌the 'ð' ​is ​the sound ​of ​English 'this' ‌or ‌Icelandic 'auður'.

​Kindred ‌and historical ​forms ​of the ‌name:

‌- **Old ‌Norse** ‌— Auðhumla, ​the ‌primeval cow ​of ​Gylfaginning
- ​**Modern ‌Icelandic** — ​Auðhumla, unchanged ​in ​spelling and ‌still ​recognizable

Auðhumla ​is ​Tier 1 ‌because ​the Norse ‌form ​preserves the ‌distinctive ​eth (ð) ‌that ‌ASCII loses. ​The ​restoration keeps ​that ​letter visible ‌in ‌the domain ​name.[^2]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌medieval Icelandic ​manuscripts ​in the ​Latin alphabet ​as **Auðhumla** ​— Old ‌Norse ​(North Germanic), ​attested 13th–14th ‌c. CE ​in ‌the codices ​of Snorri's ‌Edda (Gylfaginning ​5), recording ​material ​centuries older.[^1] ​Before the ​Latin bookhand, ‌Old ​Norse names ‌were carved ​in the ‌Younger ​Futhark; no ‌runic attestation ​of this ‌name survives, ​so ​the manuscript ‌form is ‌the primary ‌witness.

​The scholarly ​rendering proceeds ‌step by ​step:

- ​The ‌name is ​a weak ​feminine in ‌*-la*.
​- The ‌normalized Old ​Norse spelling ​uses ​the letter ​eth (ð) ‌for the ‌voiced dental ​fricative.
‌- In ​the Younger ​Futhark it ‌would ‌have been ‌carved approximately ‌ᚢᚢᚦᚼᚢᛘᛚᛅ, although ​the exact ‌runic ​spelling is ​hypothetical.
- ​The Unicode ‌form ​**Auðhumla** is ​therefore a ​scholarly normalization: ‌the ​eth distinguishes ​the Norse ​pronunciation from ‌the plain ​ASCII ‌form.

Because ​the name ‌is transmitted ​only ‌in medieval ‌manuscripts, its ​form is ​a normalized ​scholarly ​spelling rather ‌than an ‌attested runic ​carving.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 5, trans. Faulkes.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Auðhumla** ​belongs to ‌the ‌Norse tradition ​as ​the primeval ​cow, ​the first ​nourisher ‌and the ​agent ​of revelation. ‌Her ​domain is ‌the ​border between ‌non-existence ​and existence: ​she ​feeds the ​giant ​from whom ‌the world ​will ‌be made ​and ‌licks the ​first ‌god from ​the ‌ice.[^1]

### ​Nourishment

​Her milk ‌sustains ‌Ymir through ‌the ​timeless ages ​before ‌the creation ​of ​the world.

‌### ​Cosmogony

By ​licking ‌the rime-stones ​she ‌uncovers Búri, ​setting ​in motion ​the ​genealogy that ‌produces ‌Óðinn and ​his ‌brothers.

### ​The ​Primeval Animal

‌She ‌is not ‌a ‌domestic beast ​but ‌a cosmic ​one, ​belonging to ​the ‌same pre-creation ​order as ​Ymir ​and the ‌rime ​of Ginnungagap.

​### ​Generation from ‌the ​Void

Her ‌emergence ​from the ‌melting ​rime embodies ‌the ‌Norse idea ​that ​life arises ​from ​the meeting ‌of ‌fire and ​ice.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 5, trans. Faulkes.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford University Press, 2001).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Auðhumla's mythology ​is told almost entirely ‌in a single chapter ‌of Snorri's *Gylfaginning*, but ​that chapter is foundational ​for the whole ​Norse cosmos.[^1]

### Birth ​from the Rime (Gylfaginning ​5)

Snorri describes the ‌primordial landscape: to the ​north was Niflheimr, ​cold and misty, and ‌to the south Múspell, ​hot and fiery. Between ‌them lay Ginnungagap, the ​yawning void. The heat ‌from Múspell met ​the ice from Niflheimr, ​and the melting rime ​dripped into the void, ​gradually taking the shape ​of a living ‌creature: Ymir, the first ​giant. As the rime ‌continued to melt, a ​cow emerged, greater than ‌any cow on ​earth, and her name ‌was Auðhumla.[^2]

### Nourishment ​of Ymir

Auðhumla fed ‌Ymir with her milk, ​and from his ​sweat — while he ‌slept — sprang the ‌race of male and ‌female giants who populated ​the pre-cosmic world. ​She herself fed by ‌licking the salty rime-stones. ​In this economy of ​bodies and substances, the ‌cow is the ​pivot: she transforms inorganic ​rime into organic milk, ‌and the giant transforms ​milk into the beings ‌from whom the gods ​will later differentiate ​themselves.[^3]

### The Licking-forth ​of Búri

On the ​first day Auðhumla licked ‌the stones, a man's ‌hair appeared; on ​the second day, his ‌head; on the third, ​the whole man stood ​free. His name was ‌Búri, 'produced', and ‌he was fair, mighty, ‌and the father of ‌Borr. Borr in turn ​married Bestla, daughter of ‌the giant Bǫlþorn, ​and their sons were ​Óðinn, Vili, and Vé. ​The cow's patient licking ‌thus produces the godly ​line that will ​eventually kill Ymir and ​build the world from ‌his corpse.[^4]

### Absence ​from the Poetic Edda

​Auðhumla does not ​appear in the surviving ‌Poetic Edda. Her story ​is Snorri's learned reconstruction, ‌possibly drawing on lost ​eddic poems or on ‌his own synthesis ​of cosmogonic traditions. This ‌has led scholars to ‌debate whether she is ​an old Indo-European figure ​— parallel to ​the Vedic cow of ​plenty and the primeval ‌bovine of other creation ‌myths — or a ​Snorronic invention.[^5]

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Auðhumla ​remains ‌one ‌of ​the most ​visually ​memorable ​figures ​of ‌Norse ​cosmogony. ​She appears ‌in ​modern ‌retellings, ​illustrated ‌editions ​of ​the Eddas, ​and ​popular ​media ‌whenever ​the ‌creation ​of ‌the Norse ​world ‌is ​depicted. ‌Her ​image ​— ‌a vast ‌cow ‌licking ​a ​god ‌from ​the ​ice — ‌encapsulates ​the ​Norse ‌sense ​that ‌life ​arises ​from strange, ​unromantic ​processes: ‌licking, ‌sweating, ​melting, ‌and ​violence.[^1] In ​contemporary ‌Heathen ‌and ‌Ásatrú ‌practice ​she ‌is honored ​as ​the ​first ‌nourisher ​and ​the ​ancestor ‌of the ​divine ​line. ​The ‌name ​Auðhumla ‌is ​rare as ‌a ​personal ‌name ‌but ​instantly ​recognizable ​to anyone ​familiar ‌with ‌the ​sources.[^2]

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body: The ​Prose ‌Edda ‌is ​Auðhumla's ​sole ​extended ​witness. ​*Gylfaginning* ‌5 tells ​how ​she ‌emerged ​from ‌the ​melting ‌rime ​of ​Ginnungagap, ​nourished ​Ymir ​with ‌her ​milk, ‌and ​licked ‌Búri from ​the ‌salty ​stones ‌over ​three ​days. ‌Snorri ‌places ‌her ​at ​the ‌very ​beginning ​of ‌the ​divine ​genealogy: ‌without Auðhumla, ​there ‌is ​no ​Búri, ​no ​Borr, ‌and ‌no ​Óðinn.[^1] ‌The ​prose ​is ‌characteristically ‌euhemerizing ‌and ‌systematizing, ​but ‌the image ​of ​the ​cosmic ‌cow ​has ​no ​parallel ‌in ​the ​Norse ​corpus ‌and ​must ‌reflect ​either ‌a ​lost tradition ‌or ‌Snorri's ​own ​creative ​reconstruction ​of ‌the ‌pre-cosmic ​age.[^2]
